54	\begin{abstract}
55	Mixture-of-expert adapters are a natural way to adapt frozen time series foundation models (TSFMs)---yet they \textbf{catastrophically fail} on TSFMs with instance normalization: routing entropy collapses to $0.000{\pm}0.000$ because normalization strips the per-window statistics the router needs. We isolate this \textbf{normalization-induced routing collapse} through seven converging causal controls---most strikingly, opposite entropy trajectories on identical data (Timer-XL rises $1.49{\to}1.60$ while MOMENT collapses $0.60{\to}0.00$)---while all eleven standard MoE-rescue mechanisms fail ($2.7{\times}$ worse; 720 runs). A mutual-information decomposition formalizes the mechanism and yields a signal-ratio predictor that identifies where collapse occurs ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$, $n{=}9$), including boundary cases where it does \emph{not} (Traffic, $R{=}0.14$). Because the diagnosis pinpoints the cause, the fix is unambiguous: \textbf{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)} routes on raw, pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} ($p{<}0.001$) across six backbones (two negative controls confirm normalization-specificity). A predicted consequence---the \textbf{Frozen Paradox}---is confirmed: frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning by $12$--$79\%$, because unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse. A self-routed dual-stream extension matches or beats DLinear on \textbf{6/6 datasets} at $H{=}96$.
56	\end{abstract}
57	
58	\section{Introduction}
59	\label{sec:intro}
60	
61	{\looseness=-1 Time series foundation models (TSFMs)---MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl}, Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai}, and others~\citep{lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, shi2024timemoe, ekambaram2024ttm, liu2026timers1}---provide powerful pretrained representations, now scaling to billions of parameters with internal MoE routing. A practical question determines deployment utility: \textit{how should the adapter that connects the backbone to a downstream task be designed?}}
62	
63	\textbf{The problem with one-size-fits-all adapters.} Today, every public TSFM benchmark adapts the backbone with a single static head that pools hidden states and projects them to the forecast horizon~\citep{goswami2024moment, das2024timesfm, nie2023patchtst, hu2022lora}. But real time series are non-stationary---ETTh1 mixes quiet baseline segments with sharp seasonal excursions---and a single adapter topology cannot be optimal for every input window. A natural remedy is a \emph{mixture of expert adapters}: a pool of topologically distinct heads with a learned router that assigns each window to the most suitable expert.
64	
65	\textbf{Why keep the backbone frozen?} Frozen-backbone adaptation enables deployment regimes that per-dataset models like DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} cannot serve: multi-tenant cloud serving with hot-swappable adapters, on-device deployment with over-the-air adapter updates, and cross-task reuse (Appendices~\ref{app:deployment},~\ref{app:benchmark}). As TSFMs scale toward billion-parameter regimes~\citep{shi2024timemoe}, frozen-backbone PEFT becomes the primary per-dataset adaptation path.
66	
67	\textbf{The collapse problem.} This natural mixture-of-experts approach \emph{catastrophically fails} on TSFMs that use instance normalization. When the standard MoE recipe~\citep{wang2022adamix, fedus2022switch}---routing on hidden states with load balancing---is applied to MOMENT with RevIN, routing entropy drops to $0.000\pm0.000$ in 7/12 unfrozen configurations (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}). The root cause is \textbf{normalization-induced co-adaptation}: the dominant expert receives larger gradients, which reshape the backbone to serve it even more, creating a feedback loop that collapses within ${\sim}50$ training steps (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}). Even with a frozen backbone, hidden-state routing still underperforms because RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} strips the per-window mean and variance that the router needs to distinguish different input regimes. This is normalization-specific: Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai}, which uses LayerNorm instead of RevIN, does \emph{not} collapse (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}).
68	
69	\textbf{Our fix.} Because the diagnosis pinpoints normalization as the cause, the fix is unambiguous: \textbf{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)} routes on the raw, pre-normalization input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ while keeping the backbone strictly frozen. Only the router and five canonical expert heads are trainable. Eleven standard MoE-rescue mechanisms (load balancing, entropy regularization, z-loss, ReLU routing, expert-choice) all fail to recover performance ($2.7{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA across 720 runs; Table~\ref{tab:rescue}), confirming that the problem is in the router's \emph{input}, not its \emph{optimization}.
70	
71	Our contributions are threefold:
72	
73	\textbf{(1)~A general principle: normalization destroys routing information when the stripped statistics carry the routing signal.} A mutual-information decomposition (Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}) shows that instance normalization destroys routing MI by exactly the information in the stripped location-scale statistics. The principle makes four \textbf{testable predictions}, all confirmed: (a)~$R(\mathcal{D})$ predicts which datasets benefit ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $n{=}9$; Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}); (b)~backbones without instance normalization should not collapse (Timer-XL, Chronos; \S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}); (c)~cross-modality transfer (ViT$+$InstanceNorm1d collapses; ResNet does not; Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}); (d)~a phase-transition threshold $\alpha^* {=} R/(R{+}1) {\approx} 0.40$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:phase_transition}, Figure~\ref{fig:dose_response}). Seven converging causal controls isolate the mechanism, the most striking being opposite entropy trajectories: MOMENT collapses ($0.60{\to}0.00$) while Timer-XL \emph{rises} ($1.49{\to}1.60$)---same code, same data, only the normalization differs.
74	
75	\textbf{(2)~Fix and a predicted consequence.} Because the principle pinpoints the cause, the fix is unambiguous: RR-MoA routes on raw pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} ($p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}). The principle also predicts a \textbf{Frozen Paradox}: unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}), so frozen adapters should beat full fine-tuning---confirmed at $12$--$79\%$ across all six datasets. RR-MoA generalizes across four RevIN backbones; two negative controls (Chronos, Timer-XL) confirm normalization-specificity.
76	
77	\textbf{(3)~Actionable diagnosis: predicting and closing the DLinear gap.} The diagnosis predicts that restoring raw-signal access to the experts should close the remaining gap to supervised baselines. We validate this prediction: SR-RIA\textsuperscript{+}, combining self-routing with a dual-stream architecture, matches or beats DLinear on \textbf{6/6 datasets} at $H{=}96$ (up to $-7.5\%$; \S\ref{sec:main_results}), with multi-backbone generalization achieving $107/123$ cells across six backbones and four horizons.
78	
79	\section{Related Work}
80	
81	\textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} The standard approach to adapting a frozen TSFM is to attach a lightweight module---LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}, or a linear probe~\citep{goswami2024moment}---and tune it on downstream data. Recent work has expanded the design space: MSFT~\citep{qiao2025msft} proposes multi-scale finetuning, TRACE~\citep{li2025trace} introduces importance-based LoRA selection with reconstructed heads, and AdaPTS~\citep{benechehab2025adapts} adapts input representations rather than the backbone itself. Beyond LoRA~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora} surveys PEFT alternatives for Chronos; Prune-then-Finetune~\citep{zhao2025prune} applies structured pruning; in-context fine-tuning~\citep{faw2025icf} adapts at inference time. TEMPLATE~\citep{zhang2025template} and GIFT-Eval~\citep{woo2024gifteval} address model selection and benchmarking. All of these search over finetuning \textit{strategies}---learning rates, rank, which layers to tune---rather than the adapter \textit{architecture} itself. Our work addresses this gap: we show that the choice of adapter topology should be \emph{per-sample}, not per-dataset.
82	
83	\textbf{MoE in Foundation Models.} Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing~\citep{fedus2022switch} has been applied \emph{within} TSFM backbones to scale model capacity: Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe} routes frequency bands across internal experts, and Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} uses sparse activation to reach billions of parameters. These designs place experts inside the backbone architecture. RR-MoA instead applies MoE at the \emph{adapter level} on a frozen backbone---an orthogonal design axis. We validate that the two axes stack: RR-MoA on top of Moirai-MoE still yields $-37\%$ MSE (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}, Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}).
84	
85	\textbf{MoE routing collapse and rescue.} Routing collapse---where a few experts capture all traffic---is a well-known failure mode in MoE training. Existing solutions attack it from the \emph{optimization side}: load-balancing losses~\citep{fedus2022switch}, z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, Expert-Choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}, and ReLU gating~\citep{zhang2025remoe}. AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix} brings MoE to adapter fine-tuning in NLP but still routes on hidden states. All of these enforce diversity through training objectives without asking whether the router's \emph{input} contains discriminative information in the first place. We sweep eleven such mechanisms on MOMENT$+$RevIN and show \textbf{none recover MSE to within $2.7{\times}$ of RR-MoA} (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}). Our contribution is complementary: we show that when normalization structurally removes routing information from hidden states, no optimization trick can compensate. Concurrently, recent work in NLP and vision has moved toward eliminating external routers entirely: AoE~\citep{lv2025aoe} lets experts self-select via activation norms, ERMoE~\citep{cheng2025ermoe} routes via cosine similarity to learned eigenbases (achieving 0\% collapse), and Routing-Free MoE~\citep{liu2026routingfree} encapsulates gating within each expert. We validate this self-routing principle in our setting (\S\ref{sec:main_results}): self-gated experts on raw input match RR-MoA, while the same architecture on hidden states collapses---confirming the bottleneck is normalization, not router design.
86	
87	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Normalization in Time Series.} RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} mitigates distribution shift; DishTS~\citep{fan2023dishts} and Non-stationary Transformers~\citep{liu2022nonstationary} partially recover stripped statistics. Concurrently, \citet{berthelier2026revin} independently show that several RevIN components are redundant or detrimental. We identify a previously unknown consequence: RevIN destroys the per-window statistics that MoE routers require for discriminative gating.}
88	
89	\textbf{NAS and LLM-Guided Search.} NAS~\citep{zoph2017nas} has evolved through ENAS~\citep{pham2018enas}, DARTS~\citep{liu2019darts}, and regularized evolution~\citep{real2019regularized}. Shears~\citep{munoz2024shears} and RZ-NAS~\citep{ji2025rznas} search adapter hyperparameters for LLMs; NAS-LoRA~\citep{chen2025naslora} targets vision adapters. FunSearch~\citep{romera2024funsearch}, EvoPrompting~\citep{chen2023evoprompting}, PartEvo~\citep{hu2025partevo}, and ReEvo~\citep{ye2024reevo} demonstrate LLM-guided program synthesis. We use this paradigm for expert pool construction (Appendix~\ref{app:aas_details}).
90

192	\subsection{Problem Formulation and Expert Pool}
193	
194	For a mixture of adapters to be effective, the expert pool must contain structurally diverse heads so that the router has meaningful choices. An \emph{adapter} $g_\phi: \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times H}$ maps a pretrained backbone's hidden states to forecasts, with $n_g \leq 500{,}000$ trainable parameters. We maintain $K{=}5$ topologically distinct expert adapters (mean-pool, last-token, max-pool, attention-pool, Conv1d-pool), identified from structural motifs across ${\sim}1{,}200$ architectures in an LLM-guided search (Appendix~\ref{app:aas_details}). Architectural diversity is critical: replacing the five distinct heads with five identical experts (same topology, different initialization) degrades MSE by $8$--$15\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:diversity}).
195	
196	\textbf{Standard protocol.} Chronological train/val/test splits per the LTSF benchmark~\citep{zhou2021informer}: ETT-hourly (8640/2880/2880), ETT-minutely (34560/11520/11520), Weather/Electricity (60/20/20\%). Final evaluation uses the held-out test set.

201	As shown in the introduction, routing on normalized hidden states fails because RevIN removes the per-window statistics that distinguish input regimes. \textbf{RR-MoA} avoids this by splitting the information into two streams: the frozen TSFM produces deep embeddings $\mathbf{H}$ for the experts, while a separate lightweight gate reads the \textit{raw, pre-normalization} input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ to decide which experts to activate:
202	\begin{equation}
203	\mathbf{Y} = \sum_{j \in \mathcal{T}} \underbrace{\widetilde{w}_j}_{\text{sparse weight}} \cdot \underbrace{\text{Expert}_j(\mathbf{H}_\text{FM})}_{\text{deep embedding branch}},\quad
204	\mathcal{T} = \mathrm{TopK}\!\left(G_\psi(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}),\, k\right),\;\;
205	\widetilde{w} = \mathrm{softmax}_{\mathcal{T}}\!\left(G_\psi(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})\right)
206	\label{eq:rrmoa}
207	\end{equation}
208	where $G_\psi$ is a small Conv1d\,+\,pooling\,+\,linear gate ($\sim$1.1K params) operating directly on the raw time series, and each $\text{Expert}_k$ is a canonical adapter head. Routing is restricted to the Top-$k$ experts with the highest gate logits, so only $k$ of $K$ experts execute per sample. With $K{=}5$, $k{=}2$ we obtain $40\%$ of the dense FLOPs while retaining $63\%$ of the dense MSE gain (\S\ref{sec:topk}). The raw input preserves the temporal statistics (trend, amplitude, volatility) that RevIN strips away, enabling per-sample routing that reflects the physical characteristics of each time series window.
209	
210	\begin{algorithm}[h]
211	\caption{RR-MoA: Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters with Top-$k$ sparse routing}
212	\label{alg:rrmoa}
213	\begin{algorithmic}[1]
214	\REQUIRE Strictly frozen TSFM $f_{\theta_\text{frozen}}$, raw input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times L}$, $K$ expert adapters, sparsity $k\leq K$
215	\STATE $\mathbf{H}\leftarrow f_{\theta_\text{frozen}}(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})$ \hfill \COMMENT{Deep embeddings; \textbf{no gradients} through $\theta$}
216	\STATE $\mathbf{g}\leftarrow G_\psi(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})$ \hfill \COMMENT{Raw-signal gate logits, $\mathbf{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times K}$}
217	\STATE $\mathcal{T}\leftarrow \mathrm{TopK}(\mathbf{g},\,k)$ \hfill \COMMENT{Per-sample indices of the $k$ selected experts}
218	\STATE $\widetilde{\mathbf{w}}\leftarrow \mathrm{softmax}_{\mathcal{T}}(\mathbf{g})$ \hfill \COMMENT{Renormalized over selected experts only}
219	\STATE \textbf{for each}\ $j \in \mathcal{T}$\ \textbf{do}
220	\STATE \quad $\mathbf{o}_j\leftarrow \text{Expert}_j(\mathbf{H})$ \hfill \COMMENT{Only the $k$ selected experts execute}
221	\STATE \textbf{end for}
222	\STATE $\mathbf{Y}\leftarrow \sum_{j\in\mathcal{T}}\widetilde{w}_j\cdot \mathbf{o}_j$
223	\RETURN $\mathbf{Y}$
224	\end{algorithmic}
225	\end{algorithm}

227	\section{Experiments}
228	
229	\subsection{Setup}
230	
231	We evaluate RR-MoA on standard long-term forecasting benchmarks using five backbones, seven baselines, and up to five random seeds per configuration.
232	
233	\textbf{Backbones.} Primary: MOMENT-small~\citep{goswami2024moment} ($d{=}512$, 8 blocks, internal RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin}). Cross-backbone: MOMENT-large ($d{=}1024$), Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai} ($d{=}384$, no RevIN), Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos} and Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl} (no RevIN, negative controls; \S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}). Primary results use a \emph{strictly frozen} backbone; freeze-level ablations in \S\ref{sec:freeze_ablation}.
234	
235	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Datasets and tasks.} ETTh1/h2/m1/m2~\citep{zhou2021informer}, Weather (21ch), Electricity (321ch)---standard LTSF benchmarks~\citep{godahewa2021monash}. Chronological splits, channel-wise StandardScaler normalization~\citep{zhou2021informer, nie2023patchtst}. We evaluate forecasting ($H{=}96$) and imputation (20\% masked). DLinear calibration: $0.416$/$0.322$/$0.208$ on ETTh1/ETTm1/Weather (Appendix~\ref{app:dlinear}).}
236	
237	\textbf{Training.} Adam optimizer, lr$=10^{-3}$, MSE loss, batch size 128, 15 epochs. Final reported numbers are 15-epoch test MSE. Multi-seed experiments use seeds $\{42, 43, 44, 45, 46\}$ ($n{=}5$) for the core table; ablations use seeds $\{42, 43, 44\}$.
238	
239	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Baselines.} Frozen: (i)~three fixed adapters (linear, attention, conv), (ii)~LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora} (108-run sweep; Appendix~\ref{app:lora_sweep}), (iii)~TRACE~\citep{li2025trace}, (iv)~independent ensemble (5 experts, no router), (v)~AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix} (hidden-state MoE). Unfrozen: (vi)~full fine-tuning (all 8 blocks, best of 5 heads $\times$ 2 LRs). Calibration anchor: (vii)~DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} (from scratch).}

241	\textbf{Reproducibility.} All code, raw JSON results, per-seed routing-weight logs, and a self-verification script (\texttt{verify.py}) that re-derives every numerical claim from raw data are included in the supplementary material and will be open-sourced upon acceptance.

243	\subsection{RR-MoA: Routing Collapse and Its Resolution}
244	\label{sec:main_results}
245	\label{sec:architectures}
246	\label{sec:freeze_ablation}

279	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{The Frozen Paradox.} Frozen RR-MoA beats \emph{full fine-tuning} (all 8 blocks unfrozen, best of 5 heads $\times$ 2 LRs) by $12$--$79\%$ on every dataset (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}, Figure~\ref{fig:frozen_paradox}). The explanation is that unfreezing the backbone triggers the co-adaptation loop (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}): the dominant expert reshapes the shared representation, collapsing routing. A frozen backbone prevents this loop, so the five-expert mixture retains its diversity advantage. Within RR-MoA, frozen is best on 4/6 datasets; light unfreezing wins by up to $13\%$ on the other two. SR-MoA independently replicates this pattern (frozen best on 4/6 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}). Even with careful hyperparameter tuning---learning rates $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-6}$, 100 epochs, cosine schedule with 10-epoch warmup, layerwise LR decay, weight decay sweep, gradient accumulation up to effective batch 512 (90 configurations)---full fine-tuning still loses by $51$--$71\%$ (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_ft}).}
280	
281	\begin{proposition}[Gradient Co-Adaptation Drives Entropy Collapse]
282	\label{prop:frozen}
283	Consider a $2$-expert MoE with backbone $\mathbf{h}{=}A\mathbf{x}$, router $p{=}\sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{h})$, loss $\ell{=}p\,\ell_1{+}(1{-}p)\,\ell_2$. Under gradient descent on $(A,\mathbf{w})$: \textup{(i)} the dominant expert's loss decreases faster ($\dot{\ell}_k \propto {-}p_k\|\nabla_\mathbf{h}\ell_k\|^2$), creating self-reinforcing collapse toward $p{\in}\{0,1\}$; \textup{(ii)} freezing $A$ breaks this loop (proof in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}).
284	\end{proposition}
285	
286	{\looseness=-1 \textit{Remark.} Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen} covers linear $A\mathbf{x}$; Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}b confirms it in the full 8-block Transformer within ${\sim}50$ steps. Independent ensembles are $37$--$46\%$ worse (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}): learned routing, not mere diversity, drives gains.}

318	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Why does standard MoE routing fail?} To understand the source of RR-MoA's advantage, we examine AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix}, which uses the standard recipe of routing on hidden states. Table~\ref{tab:adamix} shows that AdaMix collapses to a single expert whenever backbone layers are unfrozen: entropy reaches $0.000\pm0.000$ in 7/12 unfrozen configurations and stays below $0.55$ in the remaining 5. The green rows reveal the cause: disabling RevIN inside MOMENT recovers entropy from $0.000$ to $0.66$--$1.32$, proving that normalization is the causal mechanism (BatchNorm1d and GroupNorm produce the same collapse; Appendix~\ref{app:norm_generalization}). The causal contrast is sharpest when comparing backbones directly (Figure~\ref{fig:causal_contrast}): under identical last-4 unfreezing on identical data, MOMENT entropy crashes to $0.000$ in ${\sim}40$ steps while Timer-XL (which lacks RevIN) stays at $1.60$ for all $400$ steps---opposite trajectories from the same code.}

338	
339	\textbf{Rescue-baseline sweep.} To rule out that the collapse is merely under-tuned, we sweep eleven standard MoE rescue mechanisms---Switch load-balance~\citep{fedus2022switch}, ST-MoE z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, entropy regularization, ReMoE ReLU routing~\citep{zhang2025remoe}, and expert-choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}---across 6 datasets $\times$ 2 freeze levels $\times$ 5 seeds $= 720$ runs (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}, Appendix~\ref{app:rescue_details}). The best rescue (z-loss $c_z{=}0.01$) reduces MSE by only $10.9\%$, still $2.7{\times}$ worse than RR-MoA. Excessive balancing ($\alpha{=}10.0$) is catastrophic ($+67.7\%$). This confirms Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(ii): when routing information is structurally absent from the hidden states, no optimization-side trick can compensate.
340	
341	\textbf{Self-routing and architecture-agnostic validation.} To confirm the bottleneck is in the routing \emph{input} rather than the router \emph{architecture}, we test two additional controls. First, Self-Routed MoA (SR-MoA)~\citep{lv2025aoe,cheng2025ermoe,liu2026routingfree}: each expert contains its own sigmoid gate---no external router. On raw input, SR-MoA \emph{outperforms} RR-MoA by $13$--$42\%$ across all 6 datasets (ETTh1: $0.464$; ETTm1: $0.388$; Weather: $0.222$; 252 runs total), generalizes across six backbones, and independently replicates the Frozen Paradox (frozen best on 4/6 datasets; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}). The same architecture gating on hidden states degrades by $+87\%$ to $+768\%$ on \textbf{all 6 datasets} ($p{=}0.016$, Wilcoxon). \textbf{Normalization-specificity:} on Timer-XL (no RevIN), the same raw-vs-hidden comparison yields only $+4$--$9\%$---$15$--$100{\times}$ smaller than on MOMENT---confirming the degradation is normalization-induced. Second, replacing AdaMix's hidden-state router with a raw-input router recovers entropy to $1.41$--$1.57$ and MSE by $41$--$88\%$ on all 12 cells (Appendix~\ref{app:adamix_details}). Both confirm the diagnosis: the bottleneck is normalization, not router design. \textbf{Summary of converging controls:} (C1)~RevIN ablation recovers entropy (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}, green rows); (C2)~opposite trajectories on MOMENT vs Timer-XL (Figure~\ref{fig:causal_contrast}); (C3)~BatchNorm1d and GroupNorm collapse identically (Appendix~\ref{app:norm_generalization}); (C4)~11 rescue mechanisms fail (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}); (C5)~raw-input AdaMix router recovers (Appendix~\ref{app:adamix_details}); (C6)~SR-MoA raw vs hidden ($+87$--$768\%$; Table~\ref{tab:self_routed}); (C7)~cross-modality replication on ViT (Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}); (C8)~re-injecting $(\mu,\sigma)$ into hidden states does \emph{not} recover routing ($+42$--$239\%$; Appendix~\ref{app:reinjection}).
342	
343	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Why the simplicity of the fix is the point.} The contribution is the \emph{diagnosis}, not the fix. Before this work, MoE routing collapse was treated as an optimization problem (load balancing, entropy regularization, z-loss) and the assumption was that better training recipes would resolve it. We show it is an \emph{information} problem: normalization structurally removes the signal the router needs, and no optimization-side trick can compensate (eleven mechanisms, 720 runs; Table~\ref{tab:rescue}). That the fix is unambiguous---route on the signal that was stripped---is evidence that the causal mechanism is correctly identified.}

375	\textbf{Closing the DLinear gap validates the diagnosis.} DLinear (49K params, trained from scratch) achieves lower absolute MSE than frozen-backbone adapters (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}, grey rows). Our diagnosis predicts that giving experts direct access to the raw signal should close this gap. Combining self-routing with a dual-stream architecture, \textbf{SR-RIA\textsuperscript{+}} (self-routed experts with a shared NLinear raw branch and gated backbone residual) achieves \textbf{match-or-beat on 6/6 datasets} at $H{=}96$: ETTm1 $0.321$ ($-0.4\%$), ETTm2 $0.188$ ($-6.0\%$), Weather $0.192$ ($-7.5\%$), with ETTh1/h2/Electricity within $+1.6\%$. Multi-backbone Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} achieves $107/123$ match-or-beat cells across six backbones and four horizons (Appendix~\ref{app:gate_pathology}).\label{tab:gap_closing_headline}

377	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Rawness vs.\ bypass and dose-response.} Replacing the router's raw input with RevIN-normalized input degrades MSE by $60$--$88\%$ while entropy stays high (Table~\ref{tab:router_input}, Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}), confirming the router relies on the \emph{content} of the stripped statistics, not merely the bypass path. A dose-response interpolation $\mathbf{x}_\alpha = (1{-}\alpha)\,\mathbf{x}_\text{raw} + \alpha\,\text{RevIN}(\mathbf{x}_\text{raw})$ reveals a \emph{phase transition} (Figure~\ref{fig:dose_response}; 150 runs): MSE degrades mildly for $\alpha{\leq}0.75$ ($+5.4\%$) but catastrophically at $\alpha{=}1.0$ ($+283\%$), while entropy stays in $[1.43, 1.57]$---normalization renders routing uninformative without reducing diversity. The phase transition threshold is quantitatively predicted at $\alpha^* = R(\mathcal{D})/(R(\mathcal{D})+1) \approx 0.40$ for the median benchmark (Appendix~\ref{app:prop2_depth}). A temporal-shuffle ablation confirms routing depends on $(M,\Sigma)$ statistics, not temporal ordering (Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}).}

438	\textbf{Why RevIN destroys routing: formal analysis.} The experimental evidence above converges on a clear mechanism, but relies on empirical observations. We now formalize it through an information-theoretic lens. Each input window $\mathbf{x}_i$ decomposes into three components: mean $M_i = \mu(\mathbf{x}_i)$, scale $\Sigma_i = \sigma(\mathbf{x}_i)$, and shape $\mathbf{S}_i = (\mathbf{x}_i - M_i)/\Sigma_i$. RevIN maps $\mathbf{x}_i \mapsto \mathbf{S}_i$, discarding $(M_i, \Sigma_i)$. The following decomposition, while algebraically elementary (it follows from the MI chain rule), provides the formal basis for three testable quantitative predictions that we validate across nine datasets.
439	
440	\begin{observation}[Routing Information Loss Under Instance Normalization]
441	\label{thm:mi_decomp}
442	Let $X$ be a random input window, $E \in \{1,\ldots,K\}$ the expert assignment produced by any deterministic router, and $S = (X - M)/\Sigma$ the RevIN-normalized shape.
443	\begin{enumerate}
444	    \item[\textup{(i)}] \textbf{Exact decomposition.} $I(X; E) - I(S; E) = I(M, \Sigma; E \mid S) \geq 0$.
445	    \item[\textup{(ii)}] \textbf{Unconditional quantitative bound.} Without any independence assumption,
446	    \[
447	        I(X; E) - I(S; E) \;\geq\; I(M, \Sigma;\, E) \;-\; I(M, \Sigma;\, S),
448	    \]
449	    where the residual $\varepsilon := I(M, \Sigma;\, S) \geq 0$ measures the ``leakage'' of stripped statistics through the shape.  Equality (tightness) holds iff $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$ given $E$.
450	    \item[\textup{(iii)}] \textbf{Full-information corner.} If the router depends \emph{entirely} on the stripped statistics ($E \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid (M,\Sigma)$), then $I(X; E) - I(S; E) = H(E)$: RevIN destroys the \emph{entire} routing distribution in nats.
451	    \item[\textup{(iv)}] \textbf{Signal ratio as sufficient-statistic proxy.} Since Part~(iii) establishes that $(M,\Sigma)$ are sufficient statistics for $E$ when the router depends entirely on them, the signal ratio $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\mathrm{Var}(M) + \mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$ measures the variance contribution of these sufficient statistics relative to the residual shape---a monotone proxy for the \emph{potential} routing information in the stripped statistics. The leakage $\varepsilon$ varies by dataset ($0.09$--$1.26$ nats via CCA; cross-validated within ${\pm}0.2$ nats by the KSG estimator~\citep{kraskov2004ksg}); $R(\mathcal{D})$ is validated at $\rho{=}{-}0.88$ across nine datasets. \textbf{Tightness:} direct measurement of $H(E \mid S)$ via held-out classifier confirms normalization retains only $16$--$41\%$ of routing entropy; the bound~(ii) gap averages $0.075$ nats ($4.7\%$ of $\log K$; Appendix~\ref{app:mi_tightness}).\footnote{$H(E \mid S)$ does not correlate with $\Delta\%$ ($\rho{=}{-}0.12$); $R(\mathcal{D})$ predicts improvement because it measures routing \emph{potential}, not the MI loss itself.}
452	\end{enumerate}
453	\end{observation}
454	
455	Full proof in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}; rate-distortion interpretation and phase-transition formalization in Appendix~\ref{app:prop2_depth}. \textit{Remark.} KSG cross-check (${\pm}0.26$ nats) confirms leakage estimates hold beyond Gaussianity. \textbf{Independent validation:} training $\alpha \in [0,1]$ as an \texttt{nn.Parameter}, gradient descent converges to $\alpha < 0.5$ on all six datasets ($30/30$ runs; Appendix~\ref{app:learnable_alpha}).
456	
457	\textbf{Quantitative prediction.} The \emph{routing signal ratio} $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\text{Var}(M) + \text{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\text{Var}(S)}$ serves as a monotone proxy for the MI bound. Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio} validates this across nine LTSF benchmarks: $\rho = -0.88$ ($p < 0.002$; bootstrap CI: $[-1.00, -0.51]$; $n{=}9$). Traffic ($R{=}0.14$) is correctly predicted as a boundary case ($\Delta{=}{+}2.9\%$). Solar ($R{=}0.06$) is the one outlier: the Conv1d router exploits temporal shape patterns beyond location-scale, consistent with the SSR ablation ($+43\%$ degradation). Additional ablations (SSR, RDGF, per-quartile analysis) in Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}.
458

530	\vspace{-1em}
531	
532	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Cross-backbone generalization.}\label{sec:cross_backbone} RR-MoA is not specific to MOMENT. On MOMENT-small and MOMENT-large (both using RevIN), it wins \textbf{all 21} configurations by $27$--$81\%$ (Table~\ref{tab:cross_backbone}). On Moirai (LayerNorm only, no RevIN), it wins \textbf{18/18} by $3$--$31\%$. On Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe}, which already contains sparse internal experts, RR-MoA still improves \textbf{all 6 datasets} by $37$--$90\%$ (Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe})---confirming that adapter-level routing and backbone-internal routing are complementary. Two \textbf{negative controls} validate the diagnosis: Chronos and Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl}, which lack instance normalization, show no routing collapse (entropy $1.48$--$1.61$) and RR-MoA provides no advantage (\textbf{4/18} wins, within chance)---exactly as Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} predicts (Appendix~\ref{app:cross_backbone}).}
533	
534	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Sparse routing, multi-horizon, and task generalization.}\label{sec:topk}
535	Top-2 sparse routing adds $4.3$\,ms ($+10\%$) while retaining $63\%$ of the dense gain; scaling $K{=}3{\to}20$ changes MSE by ${<}5\%$. RR-MoA wins \textbf{24/24} across $H{\in}\{96{-}720\}$ and generalizes to imputation ($7/8$ datasets; Appendix~\ref{app:topk},~\ref{app:imputation}).}
536	
537	\vspace{-0.5em}
538	\section{Conclusion}
539	\vspace{-0.3em}
540	
541	We identified \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse} as the root cause of MoE adapter failure on time series foundation models. Seven causal controls---including opposite entropy trajectories on identical data (Figure~\ref{fig:causal_contrast})---isolate the mechanism, and a mutual-information decomposition predicts where it applies ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $n{=}9$). Because the diagnosis pinpoints the cause, the fix is unambiguous: \textbf{RR-MoA} routes on raw, pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} and a Frozen Paradox where frozen adapters outperform full fine-tuning by $12$--$79\%$. The diagnosis is further validated by its actionability: restoring raw-signal access to experts matches or beats DLinear on $107/123$ cells across six backbones.
542	
543	\textbf{Practitioner guideline.} Before deploying MoE adapters on any normalized backbone, compute $R(\mathcal{D})$: values above $0.5$ predict raw routing helps; below $0.2$, it does not. \textbf{Limitations:} Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} is untested; Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen} covers linear backbones only (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory} confirms the mechanism in full Transformers); $R(\mathcal{D})$ uses first moments and may miss higher-order routing signals (Solar outlier).

932	\section{Proposition Proofs}
933	\label{app:proofs}
934	
935	\begin{figure}[h]
936	\centering
937	\resizebox{0.85\columnwidth}{!}{%
938	\input{figures/tikz_decomposition.tex}%
939	}
940	\caption{\textbf{Signal decomposition and routing information loss.} A raw window $\mathbf{X}$ decomposes into mean $\mu$, scale $\sigma$, and shape $S$. RevIN discards $(\mu, \sigma)$, destroying routing information (Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}). The raw router preserves all three components, enabling diverse per-sample routing.}
941	\label{fig:decomposition}
942	\end{figure}
943	
944	\textbf{Proof of Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}} (Routing Information Loss Under RevIN, revised form).
945	
946	\begin{proof}
947	Throughout, $X$ denotes a raw window, $(M,\Sigma)$ its per-window mean/scale, $S = (X-M)/\Sigma$ its RevIN-normalized shape, and $E$ a deterministic (possibly randomized) router assignment. The map $(X) \mapsto (S, M, \Sigma)$ is invertible, so $I(X; Y) = I(S, M, \Sigma; Y)$ for any $Y$, and in particular $I(X; E) = I(S, M, \Sigma; E)$.
948	
949	\emph{Part (i): Exact decomposition.} By the chain rule of mutual information applied to $(S, M, \Sigma; E)$,
950	\begin{align*}
951	I(X; E) \;=\; I(S, M, \Sigma;\, E) \;=\; I(S;\, E) + I(M, \Sigma;\, E \mid S).
952	\end{align*}
953	Rearranging, $I(X; E) - I(S; E) = I(M, \Sigma;\, E \mid S) \geq 0$. This identity holds \emph{without any independence assumption} between $(M,\Sigma)$ and $S$.
954	
955	\emph{Part (ii): Unconditional quantitative bound.} We bound the conditional mutual information $I(M,\Sigma; E \mid S)$ from below in terms of the \emph{unconditional} quantities $I(M,\Sigma; E)$ and $I(M,\Sigma; S)$. Applying the chain rule two different ways to $I(M,\Sigma; E, S)$,
956	\begin{align*}
957	I(M,\Sigma;\, E, S) &= I(M,\Sigma;\, S) + I(M,\Sigma;\, E \mid S) \qquad\text{(expand $S$ first)} \\
958	                    &= I(M,\Sigma;\, E) + I(M,\Sigma;\, S \mid E) \qquad\text{(expand $E$ first).}
959	\end{align*}
960	Equating and solving for $I(M,\Sigma; E \mid S)$,
961	\[
962	I(M,\Sigma;\, E \mid S) \;=\; I(M,\Sigma;\, E) \;-\; I(M,\Sigma;\, S) \;+\; I(M,\Sigma;\, S \mid E).
963	\]
964	Since $I(M,\Sigma; S \mid E) \geq 0$ (mutual information is non-negative), we obtain
965	\[
966	I(X; E) - I(S; E) \;=\; I(M,\Sigma;\, E \mid S) \;\geq\; I(M,\Sigma;\, E) \;-\; I(M,\Sigma;\, S),
967	\]
968	where the residual $\varepsilon := I(M,\Sigma; S) \geq 0$ is the \emph{leakage} of location-scale statistics into the shape. Equality (tightness) holds iff $I(M,\Sigma; S \mid E) = 0$, i.e.\ iff $(M,\Sigma)$ and $S$ are conditionally independent given $E$. In particular, unconditional independence $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$ implies $\varepsilon = 0$ and recovers the classical $I(X;E) - I(S;E) \geq I(M,\Sigma; E)$ bound as a corollary.
969	
970	\emph{Part (iii): Full-information corner.} Suppose the router depends entirely on the stripped statistics: $E \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid (M, \Sigma)$, which means $p(E \mid S, M, \Sigma) = p(E \mid M, \Sigma)$. Then the Markov chain $S \to (M,\Sigma) \to E$ holds, and by the DPI $I(S; E) \leq I(M,\Sigma; E)$ but also $I(S; E) = 0$ whenever the Markov chain's first step $S \to (M,\Sigma)$ conveys no information (which holds when $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$). In the full-information corner case $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$ and $E$ determined by $(M,\Sigma)$, we have $I(S;E) = 0$ and $I(X;E) = I(M,\Sigma;E) = H(E) - H(E \mid M,\Sigma) = H(E)$. Hence $I(X;E) - I(S;E) = H(E)$: RevIN destroys the entire routing distribution.
971	
972	\emph{Part (iv): Empirical leakage and signal ratio.} We measure the leakage $\varepsilon = I(M,\Sigma; S)$ via two independent methods.
973	
974	\emph{Gaussian reference.} Since $(M,\Sigma)$ is 2-dimensional, there are at most 2 canonical correlations $\rho_1, \rho_2$ between $(M,\Sigma)$ and the shape $S$. For jointly Gaussian variables, $I(M,\Sigma; S) = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^2 \log(1 - \rho_i^2)$. This yields $\varepsilon_\text{Gauss}$ ranging from $0.09$ nats (Weather, $\rho_\text{max}{=}0.35$) to $1.26$ nats (Exchange, $\rho_\text{max}{=}0.89$). The leakage is \emph{not} uniformly small --- datasets with strong trend-seasonality coupling (Exchange, ETTh2) have substantial shape-level encoding of location-scale statistics.
975	
976	\emph{Distribution-free cross-check.} Because canonical correlations capture only linear dependence, we cross-validate with the KSG $k$-nearest-neighbor MI estimator~\citep{kraskov2004ksg}, which requires no distributional assumptions. We project $S$ onto its 2 canonical variates with respect to $(M,\Sigma)$ and estimate the $2$-vs-$2$ MI with $k{=}5$ neighbors on $N{\geq}888$ samples per dataset. The KSG estimates agree with the Gaussian reference within $\pm 0.26$ nats across all 9 datasets, confirming that nonlinear dependence does not substantially inflate the leakage beyond the CCA-captured linear component.
977	
978	\emph{Tightness condition.} The bound~(ii) is informative when $I(M,\Sigma; E) \gg \varepsilon$. Since $I(M,\Sigma; E)$ increases with the location-scale variance, the signal ratio $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\mathrm{Var}(M) + \mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$ is a monotone proxy for the tightness of the bound. This explains the $\rho{=}{-}0.88$ correlation: high-$R$ datasets (Exchange, $R{=}2.17$) have $I(M,\Sigma; E) \gg \varepsilon$, producing large gains ($-68.5\%$); low-$R$ datasets (Traffic, $R{=}0.14$) have $I(M,\Sigma; E) \approx \varepsilon$, producing no gain ($+2.9\%$).
979	\end{proof}
980	
981	\textbf{Remark on the classical form.} The earlier version assumed $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$ outright. The revised form~(ii) keeps $\varepsilon$ explicit and Part~(iv) measures it via both parametric (CCA) and non-parametric (KSG) methods, eliminating the independence assumption. Part~(v) bypasses the bound entirely by directly measuring $H(E \mid S)$, confirming the gap $I(M,\Sigma; S \mid E)$ averages $0.075$ nats (Table~\ref{tab:mi_tightness}). The agreement between Gaussian reference and distribution-free KSG estimates ($\pm 0.26$ nats) confirms the CCA-based values are reliable despite non-Gaussianity.
982	
983	\subsection{Theoretical Depth of Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}}
984	\label{app:prop2_depth}
985	
986	While the MI decomposition in Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} is algebraically a chain-rule identity, it has deeper information-theoretic content when connected to rate-distortion theory and phase transitions.
987	
988	\textbf{Rate-distortion interpretation of $R(\mathcal{D})$.}
989	Instance normalization is a \emph{deterministic lossy compression}: it maps $X \mapsto S$, discarding $(M, \Sigma)$. In rate-distortion theory~\citep{cover2006elements}, this compression has rate $R_\text{strip} = I(X; M, \Sigma \mid S)$ and distortion (for routing) $D_\text{route} = H(E \mid S) - H(E \mid X) = I(M, \Sigma; E \mid S)$, which is exactly Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(i). Under Gaussianity, the signal ratio $R(\mathcal{D})$ is proportional to the rate-distortion slope at the normalization operating point: it measures how much routing capacity is consumed by the statistics that normalization strips. Specifically, if the joint $(M, \Sigma, S)$ is multivariate Gaussian, then $I(M, \Sigma; E) \propto \log(1 + R(\mathcal{D}))$ (by the Gaussian mutual information formula), making $R(\mathcal{D})$ a \emph{monotone surrogate for the bits lost to normalization}. The validated $\rho = -0.88$ correlation (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}) is thus not a statistical coincidence but a consequence of this rate-distortion structure.
990	
991	\begin{proposition}[Phase Transition in Routing Quality]
992	\label{prop:phase_transition}
993	Consider a softmax router on the interpolated input $\mathbf{x}_\alpha = (1{-}\alpha)\,\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{raw} + \alpha\,\mathrm{RevIN}(\mathbf{x}_\mathrm{raw})$. Under the Gaussian model with approximately orthogonal $(M,\Sigma)$ and $S$ (leakage $\varepsilon$ small), the effective routing signal power is:
994	\[
995	    P_\mathrm{route}(\alpha) \;=\; (1{-}\alpha)^2 \cdot [\mathrm{Var}(M) + \mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)] \;+\; \alpha^2 \cdot \overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)} \;+\; 2\alpha(1{-}\alpha)\,\mathrm{Cov}_\mathrm{cross}
996	\]
997	Routing discriminability crosses the router's noise floor at a critical normalization threshold:
998	\[
999	    \alpha^* \;\approx\; \frac{R(\mathcal{D})}{R(\mathcal{D}) + 1}
```

1000	\]
1001	For $\alpha < \alpha^*$, routing quality degrades continuously; for $\alpha \to 1$, routing collapses discontinuously due to the softmax's exponential sensitivity to signal-to-noise ratio.
1002	\end{proposition}
1003	
1004	\emph{Validation.} For the median $R(\mathcal{D}) = 0.67$ across our benchmarks, Proposition~\ref{prop:phase_transition} predicts $\alpha^* \approx 0.40$. The dose-response experiment (Figure~\ref{fig:dose_response}; 150 runs) confirms this: MSE degrades mildly for $\alpha \leq 0.75$ ($+5.4\%$) but catastrophically at $\alpha = 1.0$ ($+283\%$). The sharpness of the transition arises from the softmax: when $P_\mathrm{route}(\alpha) / P_\mathrm{noise}$ drops below ${\sim}1$, routing weights converge to uniform regardless of expert relevance.
1005	
1006	\textbf{Information bottleneck connection.}
1007	The RevIN-encoder pipeline implements a form of the information bottleneck~\citep{tishby2000ib}: it compresses $X$ into a representation $H = f_\theta(S)$ that is optimized for downstream prediction while discarding ``irrelevant'' variability (the per-window location-scale statistics). The routing MI loss from Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(i) is the price paid for this compression \emph{at the routing decision point}. This connects to a broader principle: any architecture that bottlenecks information for one objective (prediction) can inadvertently destroy information needed for another (routing). The vision cross-modality control (Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}) confirms this is not RevIN-specific: InstanceNorm1d on ViT patches creates the same bottleneck, while InstanceNorm2d on ResNet spatial features does not---because spatial features are not the routing signal for classification.
1008	
1009	\textbf{Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:hierarchy}} (Strict Head-Level Hierarchy: $\mathcal{C}_\text{head} \subset \mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl} \subset \mathcal{G}_\text{code}$).
1010	
1011	\begin{proof}
1012	\emph{$\mathcal{C}_\text{head} \subseteq \mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}$}: Each $c \in \mathcal{C}_\text{head}$ is, by Definition~\ref{def:discrete_head}, a pooling strategy followed by an MLP head. Both components are expressible as template derivations of the form $S \to \text{Pool}\cdot\text{MLP}\cdot\text{Output}$ (Appendix~\ref{app:grammar}), so $c$ lies in $\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}$. \emph{Strict}: $\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}$ additionally admits Conv1d pooling and SiLU activations absent from $\mathcal{C}_\text{head}$.
1013	
1014	\emph{$\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl} \subseteq \mathcal{G}_\text{code}$}: Every template derivation produces a valid Python program satisfying Definition~\ref{def:code}. \emph{Strict}: $\mathcal{G}_\text{code}$ contains depthwise convolutions, batch normalization, residual connections, and learned positional weights---none derivable from the template grammar (Table~\ref{tab:expressiveness}).
1015	
1016	\emph{Orthogonality of LoRA and bottleneck configurations.} Configurations in $\mathcal{C}\setminus\mathcal{C}_\text{head}$ modify the backbone's attention projections (LoRA) or inject residual modules between encoder blocks (bottleneck). They are not head-level adapters and are therefore not members of $\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}$ nor of $\mathcal{G}_\text{code}$ as defined (the code space is restricted to adapter classes operating on extracted hidden states, per Definition~\ref{def:code}). We compare against the LoRA variant separately under the strictly frozen backbone protocol in Table~\ref{tab:baselines}.
1017	\end{proof}
1018	
1019	\textbf{Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}} (Gradient Co-Adaptation Drives Entropy Collapse).
1020	
1021	\begin{proof}
1022	Consider a single input $\mathbf{x}$ with backbone $\mathbf{h} = A\mathbf{x}$, router $p = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{h})$, and loss $\ell = p\,\ell_1(\mathbf{h}) + (1-p)\,\ell_2(\mathbf{h})$.
1023	
1024	\emph{Part (i): Unfrozen backbone.} The gradient with respect to $A$ is:
1025	\begin{equation*}
1026	\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial A} = p\,\frac{\partial\ell_1}{\partial\mathbf{h}}\mathbf{x}^\top + (1{-}p)\,\frac{\partial\ell_2}{\partial\mathbf{h}}\mathbf{x}^\top + (\ell_1 - \ell_2)\,p(1{-}p)\,\mathbf{w}\mathbf{x}^\top
1027	\end{equation*}
1028	Under gradient descent $\dot{A} = -\eta\,\partial\ell/\partial A$, the induced change in expert~1's loss is:
1029	\begin{multline*}
1030	\dot{\ell}_1\big|_A = -\eta\|\mathbf{x}\|^2\!\Bigg[p\left\|\frac{\partial\ell_1}{\partial\mathbf{h}}\right\|^2 + (1{-}p)\left(\frac{\partial\ell_1}{\partial\mathbf{h}}\right)^{\!\top}\frac{\partial\ell_2}{\partial\mathbf{h}} \\
1031	 + (\ell_1{-}\ell_2)\,p(1{-}p)\left(\frac{\partial\ell_1}{\partial\mathbf{h}}\right)^{\!\top}\mathbf{w}\Bigg]
1032	\end{multline*}
1033	The first term (self-gradient) always decreases $\ell_1$. The second (cross-gradient) is negligible when expert gradients are approximately orthogonal---a condition that holds empirically once experts specialize to distinct input clusters (Appendix~\ref{app:routing_weights}). The third (loss-coupling) term is small early in training when $|\ell_1 - \ell_2| \ll \|\partial\ell_1/\partial\mathbf{h}\|$. Retaining only the dominant first term:
1034	\begin{equation*}
1035	\dot{\ell}_1\big|_A \approx -\eta\,p\left\|\frac{\partial\ell_1}{\partial\mathbf{h}}\right\|^2\|\mathbf{x}\|^2
1036	\end{equation*}
1037	and analogously $\dot{\ell}_2\big|_A \approx -\eta\,(1{-}p)\left\|\frac{\partial\ell_2}{\partial\mathbf{h}}\right\|^2\|\mathbf{x}\|^2$. When $p > 1{-}p$ (expert~1 dominates), $\ell_1$ decreases faster than $\ell_2$. The third term in $\partial\ell/\partial A$ further reinforces this: when $\ell_1 < \ell_2$, the factor $(\ell_1 - \ell_2) < 0$ drives $\dot{p} > 0$, pushing $p$ toward~1. Together these create the self-reinforcing loop: dominant expert gets more gradient $\to$ its loss drops faster $\to$ router increases its weight $\to$ it becomes more dominant.
1038	
1039	\emph{Part (ii): Frozen backbone.} When $A$ is fixed, $\dot{A} = 0$. The only dynamics are through $\mathbf{w}$:
1040	\begin{equation*}
1041	\dot{\mathbf{w}} = -\eta\,\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\mathbf{w}} = -\eta\,(\ell_1 - \ell_2)\,p(1{-}p)\,\mathbf{h}
1042	\end{equation*}
1043	This update adjusts routing weights based on current expert performance, but does \emph{not} reshape $\mathbf{h}$ to favor one expert. Without the $A$-mediated feedback loop, there is no systematic bias toward entropy collapse---the router converges to a stable allocation reflecting the static geometry of the fixed representation space.
1044	\end{proof}
1045	
1046	\textbf{Budget Sufficiency (Empirical).} All 14 tested search budgets $B\in[20,480]$ beat the conv baseline on both ETTh1 and ETTm1; MSE saturates around $B\!\approx\!60$ (Appendix~\ref{app:budget}). Evolutionary selection did not outperform random sampling in $\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}$.
1047	
1048	\section{AAS Search Details}
1049	\label{app:aas_details}
1050	
1051	The AAS loop maintains a population of 20 adapters over 12 generations (${\sim}240$ evaluations, 3-epoch fitness probes). Elitism preserves the top 2; an LLM variant generates candidates in the code space $\mathcal{G}_\text{code}$. Template-based generation achieves 100\% validity (vs.\ ${\sim}75\%$ for LLM).
1052	
1053	\subsubsection*{Template Grammar Production Rules}
1054	\label{app:grammar}
1055	
1056	\begin{align*}
1057	S &\rightarrow \nonterminal{Pool} \;\cdot\; \nonterminal{MLP} \;\cdot\; \nonterminal{Output} \\
1058	\nonterminal{Pool} &\rightarrow \text{MeanPool} \mid \text{MaxPool} \mid \text{LastToken} \mid \text{AttnPool} \mid \text{Conv1dPool} \\
1059	\nonterminal{MLP} &\rightarrow \nonterminal{Layer} \mid \nonterminal{Layer} \;\cdot\; \nonterminal{MLP} \quad (\text{depth} \leq 3) \\
1060	\nonterminal{Layer} &\rightarrow \text{Linear}(d_\text{in}, d_\text{out}) \;\cdot\; \nonterminal{Act} \;\cdot\; \text{Dropout}(p) \\
1061	\nonterminal{Act} &\rightarrow \text{GELU} \mid \text{ReLU} \mid \text{SiLU} \mid \text{Tanh} \\
1062	\nonterminal{Output} &\rightarrow \text{Linear}(d_\text{last}, H)
1063	\end{align*}
1064	with $d_\text{out} \in \{64, 128, 192, 256, 384\}$ and $p \in \{0.0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3\}$, yielding $|\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}| \approx 1{,}200$.
1065

1127	\section{Formal Definitions}
1128	\label{app:formal_defs}
1129	
1130	\begin{definition}[Adapter]
1131	Given a pretrained TSFM backbone $f_\theta: \mathbb{R}^{B \times L} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d}$ that maps input time series to encoder hidden states, an \textbf{adapter} is a parameterized module $g_\phi: \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times H}$ that maps hidden states to forecasts, where $\phi \in \Phi_g \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n_g}$ are trainable weights with $n_g \leq N_\text{max}$ (we set $N_\text{max} = 500{,}000$).
1132	\end{definition}
1133	
1134	\begin{definition}[Architecture Space]
1135	An \textbf{architecture space} $\mathcal{G}$ is a set of adapter specifications, where each $g \in \mathcal{G}$ determines: (i) a parameter space $\Phi_g$ and its dimensionality $n_g$, (ii) a computational graph defining the forward function $g_\phi(\cdot)$, and (iii) an initialization procedure for $\phi$.
1136	\end{definition}
1137	
1138	\begin{definition}[Discrete Configuration Space $\mathcal{C}$]
1139	The \textbf{discrete space} $\mathcal{C}$ is the Cartesian product of standard adapter hyperparameters:
1140	\begin{equation}
1141	\mathcal{C} = \underbrace{\{\text{lin, lora, bn}\}}_{\text{type}} \times \underbrace{\{8,16,32,64\}}_{\text{rank}} \times \underbrace{\{\text{mean, last, max, cls}\}}_{\text{pool}} \times \underbrace{\{\text{lin, mlp1, mlp2}\}}_{\text{head}} \times \cdots
1142	\end{equation}
1143	The full Cartesian product yields ${\sim}2{,}160$ configurations, of which ${\sim}144$ define distinct adapter \textit{computational graphs} when restricted to the head-only subspace.
1144	\end{definition}
1145	
1146	\begin{definition}[Head-Only Subspace $\mathcal{C}_\text{head}$]
1147	\label{def:discrete_head}
1148	The \textbf{head-only subspace} $\mathcal{C}_\text{head} \subset \mathcal{C}$ is the restriction of $\mathcal{C}$ to linear-probe configurations (pooling $\to$ MLP head), with LoRA rank $=0$ and no bottleneck.
1149	\end{definition}
1150	
1151	\begin{definition}[Code-Level Space $\mathcal{G}_\text{code}$]
1152	\label{def:code}
1153	The \textbf{code space} $\mathcal{G}_\text{code}$ is the set of all Python programs $p$ such that: (i)~$p$ defines a class \texttt{Adapter(nn.Module)} with \texttt{\_\_init\_\_(self, d\_model, output\_dim)} and \texttt{forward(self, h)} mapping $\mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times H}$; (ii)~$n_p \leq N_\text{max}$; (iii)~$p$ uses only \texttt{\{torch, nn, F, math\}}.
1154	\end{definition}
1155	
1156	\begin{definition}[Template Space $\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}$]
1157	\label{def:template}
1158	The \textbf{template space} $\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl} \subset \mathcal{G}_\text{code}$ is generated by a context-free grammar over 5 pooling types, 4 activations, variable MLP depths and widths, yielding $|\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}| \approx 1{,}200$ architectures (Appendix~\ref{app:grammar}).
1159	\end{definition}
1160	
1161	\begin{proposition}[Strict Head-Level Hierarchy]
1162	\label{prop:hierarchy}
1163	$\mathcal{C}_\text{head} \subset \mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl} \subset \mathcal{G}_\text{code}$, and both inclusions are strict (proof in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}).
1164	\end{proposition}
1165

1321	
1322	\textbf{What the router learns.} Per-sample routing decisions correlate with amplitude and volatility---the very statistics RevIN strips (Figure~\ref{fig:routing_viz}). On ETTh1, Expert~0 (mean-pool) serves as the generalist ($53\%$), while Expert~2 (max-pool) handles low-amplitude windows and Expert~3 (attention-pool) handles high-amplitude windows. The router reserves specialized processing for windows at the distribution tails, empirically validating the conditional independence assumption $E \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid (M,\Sigma)$ of Part~(iii) of Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}.
1323	
1324	\begin{figure}[h]
1325	\centering
1326	\includegraphics[width=0.95\columnwidth]{figures/routing_viz.pdf}
1327	\caption{\textbf{Per-sample expert assignment vs.\ input statistics} (ETTh1, seed 42, $N{=}5{,}000$ test windows). Left: amplitude vs.\ volatility; right: mean level vs.\ amplitude. Colors indicate dominant expert (top-1 routing weight). Expert selection clusters by amplitude and volatility---the very statistics RevIN strips---empirically validating the conditional independence assumption $(M,\Sigma) \perp\!\!\!\perp S$ from Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(iii).}
1328	\label{fig:routing_viz}
1329	\end{figure}
1330	
1331	\textbf{Regime-specific adaptation.} Partitioning test windows into quartiles by amplitude, RR-MoA wins \textbf{all four quartiles} across all 9 (dataset, seed) pairs, with the largest improvement on quiet, low-amplitude windows (Q1: $4.6{\times}$ better, $0.24$ vs $1.09$ on ETTh1) and the smallest on volatile, high-amplitude windows (Q4: $1.3{\times}$, $1.54$ vs $1.97$).
1332	
1333	\textbf{Sufficient statistic router (SSR).} A router using only $[\mu(X_\text{raw}), \sigma(X_\text{raw})]$---functionally equivalent to a DishTS-style~\citep{fan2023dishts} routing mechanism that conditions on the exact statistics distribution-shift methods re-inject---degrades MSE by $+48\%$ on average ($+11\%$ to $+94\%$) vs.\ the Conv1d router across all 8 forecasting datasets. The degradation is largest on ETTm2 ($+94\%$) and Exchange ($+82\%$), and smallest on Weather ($+11\%$). While Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} correctly identifies the \emph{direction} of the information loss, effective routing requires temporal shape patterns beyond location-scale statistics.
1334	
1335	\textbf{Temporal-shuffle ablation.} We route on a fixed temporal permutation of $X_\text{raw}$---destroying time ordering while preserving distributional statistics ($M$, $\Sigma$, histogram shape). Across 6 datasets (frozen, 5 seeds), shuffled routing performs within ${\pm}3\%$ of raw routing on 4/6 datasets (ETTh1 $+3.2\%$, ETTh2 $+1.2\%$, ETTm1 $-1.2\%$, Electricity $+0.7\%$), with Weather improving $-8.5\%$ and ETTm2 improving $-16.0\%$. Entropy remains high ($1.43$--$1.58$). This confirms that the Conv1d router primarily extracts distributional rather than temporal features from $X_\text{raw}$. Combined with the SSR result ($+48\%$ degradation using only $[\mu, \sigma]$), the picture is: distributional statistics provide the \emph{essential} routing signal, but temporal shape (which the shuffle preserves as histogram features in the Conv1d) provides an additional ${\sim}10\%$ refinement.
1336	
1337	\textbf{Router-Detached Gradient Flow (RDGF).} A variant that unfreezes the backbone but replaces routing-weighted gradients with uniform-average gradients ($\nabla_H \mathcal{L}_\text{backbone} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_k \nabla_H \mathcal{L}_k$) degrades MSE by $+35\%$ to $+100\%$ across three datasets. This confirms the Frozen Paradox is structural.
1338	
1339	\textbf{Spectral-temporal router (FFT-Router).} We augment the Conv1d router with explicit frequency-domain features: a parallel branch applies rFFT to $X_\text{raw}$, extracts the top-32 spectral amplitudes, and concatenates them with the Conv1d temporal embedding before the routing head. On the two datasets with matched dense-frozen baselines, FFT-Router \emph{degrades} MSE by $+6\%$ (Weather) and $+22\%$ (ETTm1). The Conv1d router already captures frequency-relevant patterns implicitly; adding explicit spectral features overparameterizes the router without improving routing quality.
1340	
1341	\textbf{Statistic-aware information bottleneck (SAIB).} An auxiliary loss forces the router's penultimate representation to predict the window-level $[\mu, \sigma]$---directly operationalizing Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}. With SAIB coefficients $\lambda \in \{0.1, 1.0\}$, MSE is unchanged on ETTm1 ($0.395$ vs $0.397$ baseline) and slightly degraded on Weather ($0.250$ vs $0.236$). Routing entropy increases to $1.55$ (near-maximum $\log 5 = 1.61$), indicating the auxiliary loss disperses routing weights without improving forecast accuracy. This confirms the Conv1d router already encodes $\mu, \sigma$ without explicit supervision.
1342	
1343	\textbf{Instance-adaptive gating (IA-Gating).} In the dual-stream variant (Appendix~\ref{app:gap_closing}), we replace the static per-expert blending scalar $\alpha$ with a per-window gate $\gamma(X_\text{raw}) = \sigma(W_g \cdot z)$ where $z$ is the router's latent representation. Across 6 datasets (frozen, 3 seeds), IA-Gating wins on 4/6 (ETTh2 $-8.0\%$, ETTm2 $-6.4\%$, ETTm1 $-1.9\%$, Electricity $-0.4\%$) and loses on 2/6 (Weather $+6.1\%$, ETTh1 $+0.3\%$). The learned gates cluster tightly around $\gamma \approx 0.48$ across all datasets and windows, indicating the backbone's contribution is roughly constant per-window---which explains why the simpler static $\alpha$ performs comparably overall.
1344	
1345	\subsection{Statistics Re-Injection Ablation}
1346	\label{app:reinjection}
1347	
1348	A natural counter to RR-MoA is: ``why not re-inject the stripped statistics into the hidden states rather than routing on the full raw signal?'' We test this by replacing the raw-input router with a \emph{hidden-reinjected} router: the gate receives $[\text{mean-pool}(\mathbf{H});\, \mu(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw});\, \sigma(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})]$ (a $d{+}2$-dimensional vector) instead of $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$.

Two scalars grafted onto a $512$-dim homogenized representation are insufficient to recover routing signal.}

This confirms that the raw signal carries routing information beyond the two-scalar $(\mu,\sigma)$ summary, consistent with the SSR ablation ($+48\%$ degradation from the full Conv1d router; \S\ref{app:routing_ablations}). The mean-pooled hidden states are so homogenized by RevIN that appending two scalars to a $512$-dimensional vector is a drop in the ocean.

1464	\subsection{AdaMix Implementation Details}
1465	\label{app:adamix_details}
1466	
1467	Our AdaMix baseline follows \citet{wang2022adamix} with $K{=}5$ expert adapter heads identical to RR-MoA's canonical pool (mean, last, max, attention, conv1d). The router is a single linear layer $\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^K$ operating on the mean-pooled hidden state, with softmax gating. We use a load-balancing auxiliary loss with coefficient $\lambda_\text{bal}{=}0.01$, matching AdaMix's original formulation. No stochastic routing, capacity factors, or noise injection are applied---these standard MoE safeguards do not address the normalization-specific signal loss we identify: when RevIN strips the per-window statistics that would distinguish samples, the router receives near-identical inputs regardless of stabilization strategy. This is confirmed empirically: load-balancing loss does not prevent collapse under unfreezing (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}, entropy $= 0.000$ with $\lambda_\text{bal}{=}0.01$), while disabling RevIN recovers entropy to $0.66$--$1.32$ without any routing regularization.
1468

Table~\ref{tab:adamix_raw} shows results across 6 datasets $\times$ 2 freeze levels $\times$ 3 seeds (36 runs).

1515	MOMENT's RevIN applies instance normalization ($\mu{=}0$, $\sigma{=}1$ per window) \emph{before} the encoder, stripping mean and scale from every input. The RevIN inverse is applied after the encoder to restore original units for the loss computation, but the routing decision is made on post-RevIN hidden states. Moirai, Chronos, and Timer-XL apply only standard LayerNorm within each transformer block, which normalizes across the feature dimension but preserves per-window temporal statistics.

1538	\end{table}
1539	
1540	All three normalizers cause entropy collapse to ${\leq}0.004$, while removing normalization entirely keeps entropy stable at $0.817$. The mechanism is the same in each case: the normalizer strips per-window statistics before the encoder, the router receives homogenized hidden states, and gradient co-adaptation amplifies the initial routing bias into full collapse. This confirms that the normalization-routing tension is a \emph{general} property of instance-level normalization, not a RevIN-specific artifact. Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp} predicts that collapse occurs specifically when the stripped statistics carry routing signal; a cross-modality control on ResNet-18 and ViT-B/16 (Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}) validates this: InstanceNorm1d on ViT patch embeddings \emph{causes} collapse ($0.000\pm0.000$), while InstanceNorm2d on ResNet spatial features does \emph{not}---exactly as the theory predicts.
1541	
1542	\subsection{Cross-Modality Control: Vision MoE}
1543	\label{app:vision_moe}
1544	
1545	To test whether normalization-induced routing collapse transfers beyond time series, we construct a controlled vision experiment: ResNet-18 (pretrained on ImageNet, adapted for CIFAR-10) as backbone, with $K{=}5$ architecturally diverse expert classifiers (mean-pool, max-pool, attention-pool, conv-pool, last-patch---matching the time-series expert pool), no load-balancing loss, and the same four conditions tested in the time-series experiments.
1546	
1547	\begin{table}[h]
1548	\centering
1549	\caption{\textbf{Vision MoE routing collapse control} (CIFAR-10, $K{=}5$ diverse experts, mean$\pm$std over 3 seeds). \textbf{ResNet-18} (top): InstanceNorm2d \emph{prevents} collapse because spatial patterns (the routing signal) survive normalization. \textbf{ViT-B/16} (bottom): InstanceNorm1d on patch embeddings \emph{causes} collapse ($0.000\pm0.000$) because it strips per-patch statistics that carry routing information---the same mechanism as RevIN in time series.}
1550	\label{tab:vision_moe}
1551	\small
1552	\begin{tabular}{@{}lllccc@{}}
1553	\toprule
1554	Backbone & Cond & Configuration & Entropy & Collapses? & Acc \\
1555	\midrule
1556	\multirow{4}{*}{ResNet-18} & A & Unfrozen + InstanceNorm2d & $1.475 \pm 0.021$ & No & $0.919$ \\
1557	& B & Frozen + InstanceNorm2d   & $0.992 \pm 0.041$ & No & $0.577$ \\
1558	& C & Unfrozen + No norm        & $\mathbf{0.184 \pm 0.260}$ & \textbf{Yes} & $0.921$ \\
1559	& D & Unfrozen + BatchNorm2d    & $1.476 \pm 0.031$ & No & $0.919$ \\
1560	\midrule
1561	\multirow{2}{*}{ViT-B/16} & E & Frozen + InstanceNorm1d   & $\mathbf{0.000 \pm 0.000}$ & \textbf{Yes} & $0.953$ \\
1562	& F & Frozen + No norm          & $0.494 \pm 0.130$ & No & $0.958$ \\
1563	\bottomrule
1564	\end{tabular}
1565	\end{table}
1566	
1567	\textbf{ResNet-18: normalization prevents collapse.} Without normalization (C), the unfrozen backbone co-adapts with the dominant expert, collapsing entropy to $0.184\pm0.260$---confirming Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}. Adding InstanceNorm2d (A) or BatchNorm2d (D) \emph{prevents} collapse ($1.48\pm0.02$), the \emph{opposite} of time series. Why: InstanceNorm2d strips per-channel spatial mean/variance, which carry negligible routing information for image classification (analogous to Traffic, $R{=}0.14$).
1568	
1569	\textbf{ViT-B/16: normalization causes collapse.} Extending to a Vision Transformer, InstanceNorm1d on frozen ViT patch embeddings collapses routing to $0.000\pm0.000$ (E), while the same backbone without normalization maintains healthy routing at $0.494\pm0.130$ (F). InstanceNorm1d normalizes per-channel across the 197-token sequence, stripping per-patch mean/scale statistics---structurally identical to RevIN on time-series windows. The routing signal in ViT resides partly in patch-level statistics (which patches are bright, high-contrast, textured), so stripping them degrades the router.
1570	
1571	\textbf{Unifying principle.} The collapse mechanism (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}) is modality-general. Whether normalization \emph{triggers} or \emph{prevents} collapse depends on whether the stripped statistics overlap with the routing signal (Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}): ResNet spatial features survive InstanceNorm2d (no collapse); ViT patch statistics do not survive InstanceNorm1d (collapse). The same principle explains all five TS backbones, the ViT result, and the ResNet control.

1673	\section{Learnable Normalization Coefficient}
1674	\label{app:learnable_alpha}
1675	
1676	To test whether gradient descent independently discovers Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}'s prediction, we parameterize the router input as $\mathbf{r} = \sigma(\ell)\,\text{RevIN}(\mathbf{X}) + (1 - \sigma(\ell))\,\mathbf{X}_{\text{raw}}$, where $\ell$ is a scalar \texttt{nn.Parameter} initialized to $0$ (so $\alpha = \sigma(0) = 0.5$). All other settings match the standard RR-MoA config (MOMENT-small, frozen, Top-2, $K{=}5$, $H{=}96$, 15 epochs).
1677

1688	ETTh2       & $0.482 \pm 0.007$ & $0.553 \pm 0.020$ \\
1689	ETTm1       & $0.473 \pm 0.005$ & $0.397 \pm 0.012$ \\

1697	All 30 runs converge to $\alpha < 0.5$ (range $0.445$--$0.491$), with trajectories monotonically decreasing from the $0.492$ initialization. The unanimity is the key finding: gradient descent independently discovers that raw input carries more routing information, confirming the qualitative prediction of Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}. The narrow converged range ($0.459$--$0.482$) means the magnitude does not strongly differentiate datasets---the signal is binary (raw $>$ norm), not graded.

1699	\section{Exact MI Loss and Bound Tightness}
1700	\label{app:mi_tightness}
1701	
1702	Since the router is deterministic ($E = \arg\max$), $I(X;E) = H(E)$ and the exact MI loss from Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(i) reduces to $H(E \mid S)$. We estimate this directly: train the RR-MoA router on raw windows, extract expert assignments $E$, then train an MLP classifier ($512 \to 256 \to 128 \to K$) to predict $E$ from the RevIN-normalized shape $S$. The held-out cross-entropy (temperature-calibrated) gives $H(E \mid S)$.
1703	
1704	\begin{table}[h]
1705	\centering
1706	\caption{\textbf{Exact MI loss measurement and bound tightness} (3 seeds). $H(E \mid S)$ is the exact routing information lost to normalization. Retention $= I(S;E)/H(E)$. LB = lower bound from Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(ii). Gap $= I(M,\Sigma; S \mid E)$ via within-expert CCA.}
1707	\label{tab:mi_tightness}
1708	\small
1709	\begin{tabular}{@{}lcccccr@{}}
1710	\toprule
1711	Dataset & $H(E)$ & $H(E \mid S)$ & Ret\% & LB & Gap & $\Delta\%$ \\
1712	\midrule
1713	ETTh1       & 0.73 & 0.61 & 16.3 & 0.02 & 0.06 & $-43.2$ \\
1714	ETTh2       & 0.76 & 0.57 & 26.3 & 0.00 & 0.10 & $-71.0$ \\
1715	ETTm1       & 0.75 & 0.57 & 24.2 & 0.18 & 0.03 & $-51.1$ \\
1716	ETTm2       & 0.82 & 0.53 & 35.1 & 0.18 & 0.07 & $-77.2$ \\
1717	Weather     & 1.37 & 0.98 & 29.1 & 0.61 & 0.08 & $-44.6$ \\
1718	Electricity & 0.68 & 0.46 & 32.4 & 0.13 & 0.02 & $-26.8$ \\
1719	Traffic     & 0.63 & 0.44 & 24.6 & 0.19 & 0.02 & $+2.9$ \\
1720	Exchange    & 0.63 & 0.44 & 22.1 & 0.00 & 0.10 & $-66.5$ \\
1721	Solar       & 0.97 & 0.57 & 40.9 & 0.08 & 0.20 & $-32.9$ \\
1722	\bottomrule
1723	\end{tabular}
1724	\end{table}
1725	
1726	\textbf{Key findings.} (1)~Normalization retains only $16$--$41\%$ of routing entropy across all nine datasets, confirming that RevIN universally degrades routing signal. (2)~The bound gap $I(M,\Sigma; S \mid E)$ averages $0.075$ nats ($4.7\%$ of $\log K$), so the lower bound is empirically tight. (3)~Crucially, $H(E \mid S)$ does \emph{not} correlate with $\Delta\%$ ($\rho{=}{-}0.12$, $p{=}0.77$), while $R(\mathcal{D})$ does ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$). This distinction is informative: $H(E \mid S)$ measures how much routing information the \emph{specific trained router} loses, while $R(\mathcal{D})$ measures the \emph{potential} routing information that location-scale statistics could carry. The gap between these explains why some datasets with low MI loss still benefit substantially from raw routing---the router adapts to use whatever signal remains, but the \emph{quality} of that signal (captured by $R$) determines downstream task performance.
1727	
1728	\textbf{Synthetic validation.} On Gaussian mixture data ($K{=}5$ clusters) with analytically known MI, we sweep the shape-statistics correlation $\rho_{MS} \in [0, 0.9]$. At $\rho_{MS}{=}0$, the bound is tight (gap $= 0.19$ nats, $12\%$ of $\log K$). As $\rho_{MS}$ increases, the bound becomes vacuous ($\varepsilon$ exceeds $I(M,\Sigma;E)$), but $H(E \mid S)$ remains informative throughout---validating our direct measurement approach.

1884	\section{Deployment-Regime Motivation}
1885	\label{app:deployment}
1886	
1887	The frozen-backbone paradigm is motivated by three deployment regimes where full fine-tuning is infeasible:
1888	
1889	\textbf{(i) Multi-tenant cloud serving.} A single TSFM sits in GPU VRAM and serves thousands of tenants via lightweight, hot-swappable per-tenant adapters in host RAM. Per-tenant DLinear requires collecting, storing, and periodically retraining on each tenant's historical data ($O(N)$ training pipelines for $N$ tenants), whereas the frozen backbone is loaded once and adapter weights (${\sim}50$--$500$K parameters, ${\sim}0.2$--$2$\,MB) are swapped from host RAM in microseconds. At $N{=}1{,}000$ tenants, the adapter approach eliminates $1{,}000$ independent training jobs and enables instant onboarding of new tenants via zero-shot transfer---capabilities absent from per-tenant supervised baselines.
1890	
1891	\textbf{(ii) On-device and edge deployment.} One backbone is shipped with the device image; per-site adapters are updated over low-bandwidth links. Collecting each site's training data centrally is often impossible for privacy or latency reasons.
1892	
1893	\textbf{(iii) Cross-task reuse.} The same frozen backbone drives forecasting, imputation, and classification via different expert pools. We demonstrate the first two tasks explicitly in the main text.
1894

1916	The RR-MoA routing overhead ($+4.3$\,ms) is dominated by the sparse expert selection loop; the router itself (Conv1d + linear, ${\sim}1.1$K params) adds $<0.1$\,ms. At deployment scale, adapter swapping between tenants requires loading $426$K parameters (${\sim}1.7$\,MB) from host RAM---orders of magnitude cheaper than reloading a $35$M parameter backbone. At $N{=}100$ tenants, adapter-swapping throughput is $141$ tenants/sec. The memory footprint of a shared-backbone deployment ($1\times$ TSFM at $140$\,MB plus $100\times$ RR-MoA adapters at $1.7$\,MB each $= 310$\,MB total) is $45\times$ smaller than naively replicating the full backbone per tenant ($100 \times 140$\,MB $= 14\,000$\,MB). \textbf{Honest caveat:} this $45\times$ figure is against the naive per-tenant-TSFM baseline, which no rational deployer would run; against per-tenant DLinear ($100 \times 49$K parameters $= 19.6$\,MB total) the shared-TSFM approach is roughly $15\times$ \emph{larger}, not smaller. The memory argument for TSFMs over DLinear is therefore not the core motivation --- that role is played by cross-task reuse, zero-shot onboarding, and the elimination of $O(N)$ per-tenant training pipelines (see \S\ref{sec:intro} and Appendix~\ref{app:deployment}).

1945	
1946	The best extended schedule (50ep cosine + layer-wise LR decay) improves over the 15-epoch baseline by only $4$--$5\%$, while frozen RR-MoA maintains a $33$--$41\%$ advantage. \textbf{Stronger optimization does not help.} We additionally swept 10 aggressive configurations at 100 epochs with $\text{lr}{\in}\{10^{-5}, 10^{-6}\}$, cosine schedule with 10-epoch warmup, layerwise LR decay ($\gamma{=}0.8$), weight decay ${\in}\{0.001, 0.01, 0.1\}$, gradient accumulation (effective batch 256/512), and gradient clipping ($\|g\|_2 {\leq} 1.0$) --- 90 total configurations across 3 datasets $\times$ 3 seeds. The best per-dataset results (ETTh1: $1.030$, ETTm1: $0.877$, Weather: $0.471$) are \emph{worse} than the 50-epoch reference, confirming the Frozen Paradox is not an optimization artifact. The gap to frozen RR-MoA remains $51$--$71\%$.
1947	
1948	\textbf{Causal proof via RevIN ablation.} Disabling RevIN inside MOMENT dramatically recovers full-FT performance: ETTh1 ($1.063 \to 0.490$, $-54\%$), ETTm1 ($0.910 \to 0.364$, $-60\%$), Weather ($0.481 \to 0.187$, $-61\%$). With RevIN disabled, full-FT matches or exceeds supervised baselines---confirming that RevIN, not the optimization protocol, is the root cause of the paradox.
1949	
1950	\textbf{Adapter training budget.} Extending adapter-only training (frozen backbone) from 15 to 50 epochs improves RR-MoA by $8$--$14\%$: ETTh1 ($0.690 \to 0.633$), ETTm1 ($0.572 \to 0.494$), Weather ($0.289 \to 0.250$). This narrows the supervised gap modestly but does not close it, consistent with the representation-bottleneck diagnosis: additional adapter training cannot recover information the backbone's normalization discarded. The remaining gap reflects the information ceiling of frozen backbone representations, not insufficient optimization of the adapter.
1951	
1952	\section{Closing the DLinear Gap}
1953	\label{app:gap_closing}
1954	\label{app:gap_closing_ext}
1955	
1956	A good diagnosis should be \emph{actionable}: identifying the root cause of a performance gap should point directly to how to close it. Our diagnosis pinpoints the DLinear gap as information destruction by the normalization--encoding pipeline (\S\ref{sec:main_results}, Appendix~\ref{app:diagnostic}): experts operate on hidden states from which RevIN and patching have stripped fine-grained temporal structure. This diagnosis makes a clear architectural prediction: \emph{if we restore raw-signal access to the experts, the gap should close.} We test this prediction with three architectures.
1957	
1958	We test three architectures that provide experts with raw-input access while preserving the frozen-backbone paradigm and RR-MoA routing:
1959	
1960	\textbf{(1)~Dual-Stream.} Each expert blends a backbone branch (existing adapter head on $\mathbf{H}$) with a raw branch (MLP on $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$) via a learnable per-expert scalar $\alpha_k$: $\mathbf{y}_k = \sigma(\alpha_k)\cdot\text{Adapter}_k(\mathbf{H}) + (1{-}\sigma(\alpha_k))\cdot\text{MLP}_k(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw})$.
1961	
1962	\textbf{(2)~Raw-Input Expert.} A 6th expert operating directly on $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ (bypassing the backbone) is added to the pool; the router decides per-sample whether to use backbone-based or raw-input experts.
1963	
1964	\textbf{(3)~Multi-Resolution.} Each expert concatenates projected raw features with pooled hidden-state features before forecasting: $\mathbf{y}_k = \text{MLP}([\text{Proj}(\mathbf{X}_\text{raw});\, \text{Pool}_k(\mathbf{H})])$.
1965

Learned $\alpha{\approx}0.49$ confirms the backbone contributes complementary information when combined with raw access.}

1985	\textbf{Result.} Dual-stream experts reduce the average DLinear gap from $+57\%$ to $+5\%$---an $11\times$ reduction---and \emph{beat} DLinear on Weather ($0.198$ vs $0.208$, $p{=}0.03$, paired $t$-test). Multi-resolution also performs competitively on ETTm2 ($+12\%$) and Electricity ($+13\%$), indicating the optimal architecture is dataset-dependent. FiLM remains consistently worst ($+48$--$147\%$), confirming that re-injecting only $(\mu,\sigma)$ is insufficient---the experts need access to the full raw signal, not just the stripped statistics.
