```
1127	\section{Formal Definitions}
1128	\label{app:formal_defs}
1129	
1130	\begin{definition}[Adapter]
1131	Given a pretrained TSFM backbone $f_\theta: \mathbb{R}^{B \times L} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d}$ that maps input time series to encoder hidden states, an \textbf{adapter} is a parameterized module $g_\phi: \mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times H}$ that maps hidden states to forecasts, where $\phi \in \Phi_g \subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n_g}$ are trainable weights with $n_g \leq N_\text{max}$ (we set $N_\text{max} = 500{,}000$).
1132	\end{definition}
1133	
1134	\begin{definition}[Architecture Space]
1135	An \textbf{architecture space} $\mathcal{G}$ is a set of adapter specifications, where each $g \in \mathcal{G}$ determines: (i) a parameter space $\Phi_g$ and its dimensionality $n_g$, (ii) a computational graph defining the forward function $g_\phi(\cdot)$, and (iii) an initialization procedure for $\phi$.
1136	\end{definition}
1137	
1138	\begin{definition}[Discrete Configuration Space $\mathcal{C}$]
1139	The \textbf{discrete space} $\mathcal{C}$ is the Cartesian product of standard adapter hyperparameters:
1140	\begin{equation}
1141	\mathcal{C} = \underbrace{\{\text{lin, lora, bn}\}}_{\text{type}} \times \underbrace{\{8,16,32,64\}}_{\text{rank}} \times \underbrace{\{\text{mean, last, max, cls}\}}_{\text{pool}} \times \underbrace{\{\text{lin, mlp1, mlp2}\}}_{\text{head}} \times \cdots
1142	\end{equation}
1143	The full Cartesian product yields ${\sim}2{,}160$ configurations, of which ${\sim}144$ define distinct adapter \textit{computational graphs} when restricted to the head-only subspace.
1144	\end{definition}
1145	
1146	\begin{definition}[Head-Only Subspace $\mathcal{C}_\text{head}$]
1147	\label{def:discrete_head}
1148	The \textbf{head-only subspace} $\mathcal{C}_\text{head} \subset \mathcal{C}$ is the restriction of $\mathcal{C}$ to linear-probe configurations (pooling $\to$ MLP head), with LoRA rank $=0$ and no bottleneck.
1149	\end{definition}
1150	
1151	\begin{definition}[Code-Level Space $\mathcal{G}_\text{code}$]
1152	\label{def:code}
1153	The \textbf{code space} $\mathcal{G}_\text{code}$ is the set of all Python programs $p$ such that: (i)~$p$ defines a class \texttt{Adapter(nn.Module)} with \texttt{\_\_init\_\_(self, d\_model, output\_dim)} and \texttt{forward(self, h)} mapping $\mathbb{R}^{B \times T \times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{B \times H}$; (ii)~$n_p \leq N_\text{max}$; (iii)~$p$ uses only \texttt{\{torch, nn, F, math\}}.
1154	\end{definition}
1155	
1156	\begin{definition}[Template Space $\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}$]
1157	\label{def:template}
1158	The \textbf{template space} $\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl} \subset \mathcal{G}_\text{code}$ is generated by a context-free grammar over 5 pooling types, 4 activations, variable MLP depths and widths, yielding $|\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}| \approx 1{,}200$ architectures (Appendix~\ref{app:grammar}).
1159	\end{definition}
1160	
1161	\begin{proposition}[Strict Head-Level Hierarchy]
1162	\label{prop:hierarchy}
1163	$\mathcal{C}_\text{head} \subset \mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl} \subset \mathcal{G}_\text{code}$, and both inclusions are strict (proof in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}).
1164	\end{proposition}
1165	
1166	\label{app:expressiveness}
1167	\begin{table}[h]
1168	\centering
1169	\caption{Search space expressiveness hierarchy. Winning AAS architectures lie in $\mathcal{G}_\text{code} \setminus \mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}$.}
```

```
 \section{Proposition Proofs}

@@ -1006,16 +971,6 @@ For $\alpha < \alpha^*$, routing quality degrades continuously; for $\alpha \to
 \textbf{Information bottleneck connection.}
 The RevIN-encoder pipeline implements a form of the information bottleneck~\citep{tishby2000ib}: it compresses $X$ into a representation $H = f_\theta(S)$ that is optimized for downstream prediction while discarding ``irrelevant'' variability (the per-window location-scale statistics). The routing MI loss from Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}(i) is the price paid for this compression \emph{at the routing decision point}. This connects to a broader principle: any architecture that bottlenecks information for one objective (prediction) can inadvertently destroy information needed for another (routing). The vision cross-modality control (Appendix~\ref{app:vision_moe}) confirms this is not RevIN-specific: InstanceNorm1d on ViT patches creates the same bottleneck, while InstanceNorm2d on ResNet spatial features does not---because spatial features are not the routing signal for classification.
 
-\textbf{Proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:hierarchy}} (Strict Head-Level Hierarchy: $\mathcal{C}_\text{head} \subset \mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl} \subset \mathcal{G}_\text{code}$).
-
-\begin{proof}
-\emph{$\mathcal{C}_\text{head} \subseteq \mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}$}: Each $c \in \mathcal{C}_\text{head}$ is, by Definition~\ref{def:discrete_head}, a pooling strategy followed by an MLP head. Both components are expressible as template derivations of the form $S \to \text{Pool}\cdot\text{MLP}\cdot\text{Output}$ (Appendix~\ref{app:grammar}), so $c$ lies in $\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}$. \emph{Strict}: $\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}$ additionally admits Conv1d pooling and SiLU activations absent from $\mathcal{C}_\text{head}$.
-
-\emph{$\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl} \subseteq \mathcal{G}_\text{code}$}: Every template derivation produces a valid Python program satisfying Definition~\ref{def:code}. \emph{Strict}: $\mathcal{G}_\text{code}$ contains depthwise convolutions, batch normalization, residual connections, and learned positional weights---none derivable from the template grammar (Table~\ref{tab:expressiveness}).
-
-\emph{Orthogonality of LoRA and bottleneck configurations.} Configurations in $\mathcal{C}\setminus\mathcal{C}_\text{head}$ modify the backbone's attention projections (LoRA) or inject residual modules between encoder blocks (bottleneck). They are not head-level adapters and are therefore not members of $\mathcal{G}_\text{tmpl}$ nor of $\mathcal{G}_\text{code}$ as defined (the code space is restricted to adapter classes operating on extracted hidden states, per Definition~\ref{def:code}). We compare against the LoRA variant separately under the strictly frozen backbone protocol in Table~\ref{tab:baselines}.
-\end{proof}
-
```

```
54	\begin{abstract}
55	When a mixture-of-expert (MoE) adapter is attached to a frozen time series foundation model (TSFM), the router should learn to send different input windows to different experts. Instead, on TSFMs with instance normalization, the router learns to send \emph{every} window to the \emph{same} expert---routing entropy collapses to $0.000{\pm}0.000$, and the remaining experts are never used. We identify \textbf{normalization-induced routing collapse}: instance normalization strips the per-window mean and variance that the router needs to distinguish input regimes, leaving it with homogenized hidden states that all look alike. Seven converging causal controls isolate the mechanism---most strikingly, opposite entropy trajectories on identical data (Timer-XL rises $1.49{\to}1.60$ while MOMENT collapses $0.60{\to}0.00$)---and all eleven standard MoE-rescue mechanisms fail ($2.7{\times}$ worse; 720 runs). A mutual-information decomposition formalizes the mechanism and yields a signal-ratio predictor ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$, $n{=}9$) that identifies where collapse occurs, including boundary cases where it does \emph{not} (Traffic, $R{=}0.14$). Because the diagnosis pinpoints the cause, the fix is unambiguous: \textbf{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)} routes on raw, pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} ($p{<}0.001$) across six backbones (two negative controls confirm normalization-specificity). A predicted consequence---the \textbf{Frozen Paradox}---is confirmed: frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning by $12$--$79\%$, because unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse. An extension restoring raw-signal access to experts matches or beats DLinear on 6/6 datasets (Appendix).
56	\end{abstract}
```

The claim is largely accurate but "every" is risky. Let me check for counter-examples.

Standard TSFM evaluation protocols (MOMENT, TimesFM, Chronos, Moirai, PatchTST, Timer-XL) all use a single head per task. GIFT-Eval, Monash, and the Informer-era LTSF protocol all follow this pattern.

- **TRACE** (Li & Zhu 2025, also cited) uses importance-based LoRA selection with reconstructed heads

```
Now I have a thorough reading of the main body. Let me compile the over-generalization findings.

---

Here are the over-generalization claims I found in the main body (lines 1-545), ordered by severity.

---

**1. "A general principle: normalization destroys routing information when the stripped statistics carry the routing signal."**

- **Line:** 73 (Contribution 1 heading)
- **Text:** `A general principle: normalization destroys routing information when the stripped statistics carry the routing signal.`
- **Why over-generalized:** The word "general" is doing heavy lifting. The empirical evidence covers one family of instance normalization (RevIN) on one primary backbone (MOMENT), with BatchNorm1d and GroupNorm tested only on MOMENT, and a single cross-modality probe (ViT + InstanceNorm1d on CIFAR-10). LayerNorm on Moirai does NOT cause collapse. The principle has not been tested on TSFMs with other normalization variants (e.g., RMSNorm, adaptive normalization, DishTS-style partial de-normalization), nor on Time-MoE, TimesFM, or iTransformer. Calling it "general" overstates the scope of validation.
- **Suggested fix:** `A principle validated across three normalization families and two modalities: instance normalization destroys routing information when the stripped statistics carry the routing signal.`

---

**2. "For years the MoE community attacked routing collapse from the optimization side...under the assumption that better training recipes would resolve it."**

- **Line:** 343
- **Text:** `For years the MoE community attacked routing collapse from the optimization side---load balancing, entropy regularization, z-loss---under the assumption that better training recipes would resolve it.`
- **Why over-generalized:** This characterizes the entire MoE community as having operated under a single flawed assumption. In reality, routing collapse in standard MoE (GPT-4 scale LLMs, vision MoE) is typically an optimization problem that IS resolved by these mechanisms. The normalization-induced variant is specific to TSFMs with instance normalization -- it is not the same failure mode the community was trying to fix. The sentence implies the community was wrong in general, when they were right for their setting.
- **Suggested fix:** `Standard MoE-rescue mechanisms---load balancing, entropy regularization, z-loss---were designed for optimization-induced collapse and succeed in that setting. We show they cannot address normalization-induced collapse, which is a structurally different failure mode: the routing information is absent from the hidden states, not merely under-optimized.`

---

**3. "the fix is unambiguous" (appears 4 times: lines 55, 69, 75, 541)**

- **Line:** 55 (abstract), 69 (intro), 75 (contribution 2), 541 (conclusion)
- **Text:** `Because the diagnosis pinpoints the cause, the fix is unambiguous`
- **Why over-generalized:** The paper itself shows the fix is NOT unambiguous -- SR-MoA (self-routed) outperforms RR-MoA by 13-42% on all 6 datasets (line 341). The Residual-IA+ extension is needed to close the DLinear gap. The "unambiguous" fix (basic RR-MoA) still loses to DLinear on most datasets. "Unambiguous" suggests there is exactly one obvious fix, but the paper demonstrates at least three valid instantiations (RR-MoA, SR-MoA, AdaMix-Raw) with different performance profiles.
- **Suggested fix:** `Because the diagnosis pinpoints the cause, the fix principle is clear: route on raw, pre-normalization input` (drop "unambiguous" and say "clear" or "straightforward" instead, which accurately conveys that the direction is obvious without implying there is only one valid implementation).

---

**4. "frozen-backbone PEFT becomes the primary per-dataset adaptation path"**

- **Line:** 65
- **Text:** `As TSFMs scale toward billion-parameter regimes, frozen-backbone PEFT becomes the primary per-dataset adaptation path.`
- **Why over-generalized:** This is a forward-looking claim about the field that is not supported by the paper's evidence. The paper shows DLinear (from scratch, 49K params) beats frozen-backbone RR-MoA in absolute MSE. PatchTST and iTransformer (from scratch) also beat it. The paper's own results do not establish that frozen PEFT is "primary" -- they show it is useful for multi-tenant deployment, but the MSE evidence suggests from-scratch models remain competitive or superior. "Primary" implies it will be the dominant approach, which is speculative.
- **Suggested fix:** `As TSFMs scale toward billion-parameter regimes, frozen-backbone PEFT becomes an increasingly important per-dataset adaptation path.`

---

**5. "no optimization trick can compensate" / "no optimization-side trick can compensate"**

- **Lines:** 85, 339, 343
- **Text:** `when normalization structurally removes routing information from hidden states, no optimization trick can compensate`
- **Why over-generalized:** The paper tested 11 specific rescue mechanisms on one backbone (MOMENT) with one normalization (RevIN). "No optimization trick" is an absolute universal negative that goes beyond the evidence. A future optimization approach that, for instance, learns to reconstruct the stripped statistics inside the hidden state before routing (akin to DishTS-style denormalization applied to router inputs) could potentially work. The paper cannot rule out all possible optimization-side approaches.
- **Suggested fix:** `when normalization structurally removes routing information from hidden states, none of the eleven standard MoE-rescue mechanisms we tested can compensate` (the paper already uses this phrasing in some places; it should be consistent everywhere).

---

**6. "previously unknown consequence"**

- **Line:** 87
- **Text:** `We identify a previously unknown consequence: RevIN destroys the per-window statistics that MoE routers require for discriminative gating.`
- **Why over-generalized:** The paper itself cites Berthelier et al. (2026) as concurrently showing that "several RevIN components are redundant or detrimental." It is difficult to claim something is "previously unknown" when concurrent work exists on the same phenomenon. Additionally, "require" is absolute -- the paper's own evidence shows Moirai's hidden-state routing does NOT require these statistics (Moirai entropy is 1.48-1.60 without them). It would be more accurate to say MoE routers "benefit from" rather than "require."
- **Suggested fix:** `We identify a consequence not previously characterized in the MoE literature: RevIN strips the per-window statistics that substantially aid discriminative gating in MoE routers.`

---

**7. "54/54 wins across six backbones"**

- **Line:** 55 (abstract)
- **Text:** `achieving 54/54 wins ($p<0.001$) across six backbones (two negative controls confirm normalization-specificity)`
- **Why over-generalized:** The 54/54 wins are across 6 datasets x 3 freeze levels x 3 seeds on MOMENT-small only (Table `tab:rrmoa`). The "six backbones" part of the sentence makes it sound like the 54/54 is computed across six backbones, but it is not. The cross-backbone results are separate: Chronos and Timer-XL show only 4/18 wins (within chance). Placing "54/54 wins" and "six backbones" in the same sentence creates a misleading proximity.
- **Suggested fix:** `achieving 54/54 wins ($p<0.001$) on the primary backbone, generalizing across four RevIN/LayerNorm backbones (two negative controls without instance normalization confirm normalization-specificity)`

---

**8. "Today, every public TSFM benchmark adapts the backbone with a single static head"**

- **Line:** 63
- **Text:** `Today, every public TSFM benchmark adapts the backbone with a single static head that pools hidden states and projects them to the forecast horizon`
- **Why over-generalized:** TRACE (cited in the same paper) uses importance-based LoRA selection with reconstructed heads, which is not a single static head. AdaPTS adapts input representations. MSFT uses multi-scale finetuning. The paper's own related work section contradicts this "every" claim. GIFT-Eval also evaluates multiple adaptation strategies.
- **Suggested fix:** `Standard TSFM benchmarks typically adapt the backbone with a single static head that pools hidden states and projects them to the forecast horizon`

---

**9. "on every dataset" for the Frozen Paradox**

- **Line:** 279
- **Text:** `Frozen RR-MoA beats full fine-tuning (all 8 blocks unfrozen, best of 5 heads x 2 LRs) by 12--79% on every dataset`
- **Why over-generalized (mild):** This is technically supported by the data in Table `tab:baselines`, but the table only shows 3 datasets (ETTh1, ETTm1, Weather) while the claim is "every dataset" (implying all 6). The frozen paradox bar chart (Figure `fig:frozen_paradox`) does show all 6 datasets, but the reader looking at Table `tab:baselines` sees only 3. The claim is likely correct for all 6, but the main table does not verify it.
- **Suggested fix:** Either add all 6 datasets to Table `tab:baselines` or qualify: `by 12--79% on all six datasets (Figure~\ref{fig:frozen_paradox}; full grid in Appendix)`.

---

**10. "matches or beats DLinear on 6/6 datasets"**

- **Line:** 55 (abstract), 375
- **Text (abstract):** `An extension restoring raw-signal access to experts matches or beats DLinear on 6/6 datasets (Appendix).`
- **Text (line 375):** `a dual-stream extension matches or beats DLinear on 6/6 datasets at H=96`
- **Why over-generalized:** The "matches or beats" framing obscures that several of those wins are within noise (e.g., the appendix shows some are not statistically significant). Additionally, this is only at H=96; the multi-horizon results in the appendix show the picture is less clean at longer horizons. Saying "6/6" without qualification of effect sizes or significance could mislead.
- **Suggested fix:** `a dual-stream extension matches or beats DLinear on 6/6 datasets at $H{=}96$ (statistically significant on N/6)` -- fill N with the actual count of significant wins.

---

**11. "Before deploying MoE adapters on any normalized backbone, compute R(D)"**

- **Line:** 543
- **Text:** `Before deploying MoE adapters on any normalized backbone, compute R(D): values above 0.5 predict raw routing helps; below 0.2, it does not.`
- **Why over-generalized:** R(D) was validated on 9 LTSF benchmarks with one primary backbone. "Any normalized backbone" extends to architectures never tested (RMSNorm-based models, vision transformers, audio models, etc.). The thresholds 0.5 and 0.2 are derived from n=9 data points with one acknowledged outlier (Solar). This is a practitioner guideline with very thin statistical support for the specific thresholds.
- **Suggested fix:** `Before deploying MoE adapters on TSFMs with instance normalization, compute R(D): in our experiments, values above 0.5 predict raw routing helps; below 0.2, it does not (validated on 9 LTSF datasets).`

---

**12. "This is normalization-specific: Moirai, which uses LayerNorm instead of RevIN, does not collapse"**

- **Line:** 67
- **Text:** `This is normalization-specific: Moirai, which uses LayerNorm instead of RevIN, does not collapse.`
- **Why over-generalized (mild):** The phrasing implies that any non-RevIN normalization avoids collapse. But the paper only tests LayerNorm (Moirai), no-normalization (Chronos, Timer-XL), and three instance-normalization variants that DO collapse (RevIN, BatchNorm1d, GroupNorm). The claim should specify that collapse is specific to instance normalization, not just "normalization-specific" (which could be read as "specific to having normalization at all").
- **Suggested fix:** `This is instance-normalization-specific: Moirai, which uses LayerNorm instead of RevIN, does not collapse.`

---
```

```
54	\begin{abstract}
55	Time series foundation models (TSFMs) like MOMENT and Moirai provide powerful pretrained representations, but adapting them to a downstream task requires attaching a lightweight adapter head that maps hidden states to predictions. Standard TSFM benchmarks use a single static head---one adapter topology for every input window. A natural improvement is a mixture-of-expert (MoE) adapter, where a router selects the best expert head for each window. However, on TSFMs with instance normalization, this \textbf{catastrophically fails}: the router learns to send \emph{every} window to the \emph{same} expert---routing entropy collapses to $0.000{\pm}0.000$, and the remaining experts are never used. We identify \textbf{normalization-induced routing collapse}: instance normalization strips the per-window mean and variance that the router needs to distinguish input regimes, leaving it with homogenized hidden states that all look alike. Seven converging causal controls isolate the mechanism---most strikingly, opposite entropy trajectories on identical data (Timer-XL rises $1.49{\to}1.60$ while MOMENT collapses $0.60{\to}0.00$)---and all eleven standard MoE-rescue mechanisms fail ($2.7{\times}$ worse; 720 runs). A mutual-information decomposition formalizes the mechanism and yields a signal-ratio predictor ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $p{<}0.002$, $n{=}9$) that identifies where collapse occurs, including boundary cases where it does \emph{not} (Traffic, $R{=}0.14$). Because the diagnosis pinpoints the cause, the fix is unambiguous: \textbf{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters (RR-MoA)} routes on raw, pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} ($p{<}0.001$) across six backbones (two negative controls confirm normalization-specificity). A predicted consequence---the \textbf{Frozen Paradox}---is confirmed: frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning by $12$--$79\%$, because unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse. An extension restoring raw-signal access to experts matches or beats DLinear on 6/6 datasets (Appendix).
56	\end{abstract}
```

```
538	\section{Conclusion}
539	\vspace{-0.3em}
540	
541	We identified \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse} as the root cause of MoE adapter failure on time series foundation models. Seven causal controls---including opposite entropy trajectories on identical data (Figure~\ref{fig:causal_contrast})---isolate the mechanism, and a mutual-information decomposition predicts where it applies ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, $n{=}9$). Because the diagnosis pinpoints the cause, the fix is unambiguous: \textbf{RR-MoA} routes on raw, pre-normalization input, achieving \textbf{54/54 wins} and a Frozen Paradox where frozen adapters outperform full fine-tuning by $12$--$79\%$. The diagnosis is further validated by its actionability: restoring raw-signal access to experts matches or beats DLinear on $107/123$ cells across six backbones.
542	
543	\textbf{Practitioner guideline.} Before deploying MoE adapters on any normalized backbone, compute $R(\mathcal{D})$: values above $0.5$ predict raw routing helps; below $0.2$, it does not. \textbf{Limitations:} Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} is untested; Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen} covers linear backbones only (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory} confirms the mechanism in full Transformers); $R(\mathcal{D})$ uses first moments and may miss higher-order routing signals (Solar outlier).
544	
545	\label{page:end_main}
```
